speakeroldname: Mr. Russell MacLellan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate, I would like to pay tribue to Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation for the part it has played for more than 35 years in the development of mortgage financing in residential construction in this country.
CMHC introduced mortgage insurance in Canada in 1954 as a way of protecting mortgage insurers against loss, making mortgages more attractive as an investment, and as a way of making sure there was enough capital available for all of the housing which had to be built. In that year, 1954, the Bank Act was amended to allow the chartered banks to make mortgage loans. Until that time, the loans were available only from insurance companies and loan and trust companies.
The first year that CMHC offered mortgage insurance- and the corporation was alone in that field for quite a while, and certainly at that time-lending institutions approved $636 million in loans for new construction, an increase of 70 per cent over the previous year. In 1966 CMHC began insuring mortgages on existing houses as well as new construction. Nowadays with private insurers in the field, CMHC still insures nearly a third of all institutional lending for both new and existing housing.
The corporation now has $24 billion worth of mortgages insured. Its own mortgage portfolio amounts to almost $9 billion. It has played this role through the mechanism of mortgage insurance which, by enabling the introduction and use of the high ratio loan for both home ownership and rental
Housing
production, has contributed to our status among the best housed people in the world.
The legislation under which CMHC conducts its insurance business, the National Housing Act, was framed and evolved in an extended period of relatively stable growth and low inflation. That world, as we know, changed abruptly in the mid-seventies. With that change, our existing ways of financing housing no longer seemed to be appropriate.
In a time of high inflation and high interest rates, people with five-year level payment mortgages are forced to make very high payments in the early years of the mortgage. These initial high payments effectively block many young families from owning their own homes.
In the last few years interest rates have not only climbed, they have become very much more volatile as well. As a result, it is even more difficult for Canadians to buy homes. Mortgage terms have become shorter because lenders cannot attract longer-term funds. Borrowers, on the other hand, do not want to be stuck with a high rate mortgage if interest rates decline.
As we all know, many borrowers are in serious difficulty because they are suddenly faced with a sharp increase in payments on renewal. The Canada mortgage renewal plan, which this bill will authorize, will bring at least temporary relief to people who are in the most serious trouble. The most disturbing aspect of the situation, however, is the increase in uncertainty about the future of interest rates which affects both lenders and potential home buyers. This uncertainty dampens both the effective demand for housing and the supply of investment capital.
Clearly the time has come to examine alternatives to the rollover mortgages that are more appropriate to these times of high and fluctuating interest rates and to widen the choice for the borrower. 1 believe the government has a responsibility to play a role in this process. There is no shortage of ideas in the private sector. Due to legislative constraints in the National Housing Act, however, the government cannot play the essential supportive role it would like to in the process of increasing the choice of borrowing instruments and encouraging lenders to assume some of the risk for borrowers in difficulty.
The constraints that I refer to relate to the terms and conditions under which CMHC may insure mortgages, the way it may charge for that insurance and the methods by which it may settle claims on these mortgages. These three factors are all interwoven. The detailed terms and conditions specified in the act prevent the corporation from being receptive to alternative mortgage instruments proposed by builders, lenders and the public. Even if the corporation were given this flexibility, the entrenching of premiums in the act itself would prevent the corporation from charging a premium commensurate with risk. As a result it could not insure the more innovative instruments without causing a drain on the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
.. Finally, the claim settlement procedures in the act now, because of limitations on interest arrears which the lender could claim on default, discourage the lender from deferring

February 8, 1982
Housing
default action when borrowers are in temporary difficulty. In summary then, the corporation is hemmed in by legislative constraints which impede its role of ensuring that mortgage markets work well and that prevailing mortgage finance mechanisms facilitate ownership and rental investment.
1 believe that the legislative amendments will enable the corporation to be responsive to consumer needs and to the preferences and concerns of the lending industry, builders and experts in the mortgage field. They will permit CMHC to widen the choice of financing options available to the home purchaser and the investor. 1 believe that the way to a solution to the present-day difficulties in the housing sector lies to a great extent in modifications to financing mechanisms.
Back in 1954 the government showed the initiative in introducing mortgage insurance for high ratio loans to offer more Canadians the opportunity to build their own homes and more investors to build rental housing. Today we need to show initiative comparable to that shown by our predecessors in this House of Commons over 25 years ago. We face economic circumstances very different from those that they faced, and the answers are correspondingly different. The 1980s will be a time of evolving mortgage financing techniques.
The mechanism of mortgage insurance is an essential element of this evolution, but it can only play a part if the legislation is sufficiently flexible. While much of the attention of late has focused on access to ownership and renewal difficulties, we all know that the problems in the rental sector are formidable. Due to the large sums involved in financing large rental projects, public mortgage insurance plays a particularly important role.
A major impediment in this area has been the fact that cost recovery underwriting, given existing premiums, requires the investor to put up an inordinately high proportion of the required capital out of his own funds. In other words, the investor must provide an unacceptably high down payment. In today's circumstances of extremely tight rental markets, the corporation must be in a position to underwrite the size of rental loan which would make rental investment feasible.
To the extent that investors are not willing to finance rental accommodation, there is an increased demand for taxpayers' money for that purpose. The facility to set premiums commensurate with risk will enable the corporation to show more flexibility in its underwriting practices with no cost to the taxpayer.
Similar considerations apply to the ownership side. Aside from affordability, the question of uncertainty is a major consideration for purchasers. With some imagination, mechanisms can be developed which transfer some of the interest-rate risk from the home buyer to the mortgage lender. I think this is extremely significant. The lender's risk can then be underwritten by the government on payment of the appropori-ate premium.
Mortgage insurance is there because mortgage lending is, and always has been, a risky proposition. It will remain a risky
proposition. The bill before us today is designed to ensure that money continues to flow into housing in a way that provides the home buyer with the widest possible choice of how he or she will borrow the money and on what terms he or she will pay it back.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, would the parliamentary secretary permit a question? I do not believe that his time is up.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is that agreed?
Agreed.

Could the parliamentary secretary tell us if one of the contemplated schemes in the act is to have Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation guarantee a fixed rate of interest for five years upon the payment of an appropriate insurance fee?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in answer to the question of the hon. member, I would say that it would be one point of view which we could consider in committee.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that members on the opposite side have come forward with a bill to amend the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act and the National Housing Act. Members of the House will now have an opportunity to give serious consideration to the problems which face home owners from coast to coast. No member of the House denies that these problems are serious.
In his introductory remarks, the minister spoke of the urgency of the bill and the opportunity it will give to young people to acquire new homes. I agree with the urgency and the necessity for the House to make it possible for those who already own homes to be able to continue to do so. However, I do not see any provision in the amendments to either act to make it easier for any person, young or old, to buy a new home.
The minister spoke positively and in rather glowing terms about how the provisions will make it possible for home owners in Canada to purchase homes as a result of the flexibility in the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. But the amendment which was brought forward simply reflects an outdated budget which was brought in on November 12, a budget which was an established disaster and disappointment in the eyes of most people across Canada.
It is my hope that the flexibility which the minister says will be introduced in this legislation will enable people who purchased a home under the AHOP agreement five or six years ago at affordable mortgage rates to stay in their homes. I hope this flexibility will allow those home owners to be given the same financial opportunity as the entrepreneur down the street. Even if these home owners do not qualify under the provisions of the 30 per cent shelter cost ratio, I hope they would be able to become a tenant on the property which they have been paying for over the years rather than having to
February 8, 1982

move and rent another CME1C accommodation down the street. This practice has happened in the past. 1 trust that it will not continue in the future.
At the outset, I would like to say that it is a pretty sad commentary on the state of our economy and the actions of the government when home owner and builder alike are in such dire straits that the minister responsible for housing must ask for speedy passage of this bill. The bill may not offer much, they say, but it is all there is or will be. In other words, the home owner and builder have given up expecting anything but platitudes and empty promises from the government.
Reference has already been made to the letter addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) by ten members of his own government. I would like to quote two paragraphs from that letter:
It is well known that the construction industry creates numerous jobs in related fields in addition to the direct jobs that it produces. In view of the present slump in the construction industry, we think that incentives in this area would have beneficial, stimulating effects on the job situation throughout the country.
By putting emphasis on the construction of homes we would be killing two birds with one stone since such a step would help to make up for the deficit of the 50,000 housing units suffered by Canada in 1981.
Last summer and fall, the minister of housing saw fit to raise the hopes and dreams of home owners by making vague and cryptic comments about an assistance program which would soon be forthcoming. He was obviously thinking about the November 12 budget without giving the date it would be brought down. The heart of this campaign, a campaign born of the bunker, was reached on September 15 when the minister met with representatives of the "Convoy of Anger", or the Save Our Homes Campaign Committee. His message to these outraged home owners was quite clear and specific: "Help is on the way." That message was repeated over and over again throughout September, October and the first days of November until even members on this side of the House, as well as myself, being an optimist by nature, took it as a statement we could follow and we urged our constituents to hold off giving up on their homes and to wait until budget night.
We should have known better. The assistance program which was announced on budget night and is under discussion today gives new meaning to the phrase, "Well, that is the least that could be done." Under this program, a home owner must go hat in hand to the mortgage holder at renewal time-but only at renewal time-and set out his personal financial life in detail. If it is found that the principal and interest payments on the mortgage plus property tax and, if applicable, half of the condominium common element costs exceed 30 per cent of the household income, then negotiations might begin. However, those negotiations are really just between the government and the mortgage holder. If both are agreed that the home owner qualifies for assistance and both are prepared to assist, it is then determined how much equity that home owner has built up in his property, and if that equity is sufficient to permit an increase in the mortgage, the mortgagee may increase that mortgage up by a further $3,000. The amount of the increase is deducted from the annual payable interest.
Therefore, if a home owner's mortgage payments were to increase from $400 to $600 per month and that home owner
Housing
qualified for assistance, $2,400 would be added to his or her mortgage payments for one year. The mortgage payment would remain at $400 per month. But in the instance of the home owner being without equity and subject to the criteria that was mentioned earlier, CMHC will pay the mortgage holder up to $3,000 to offset the increase in the monthly mortgage payment that the home owner is unable to meet. CMHC's contribution is not repayable by either the home owner or the mortgagee. That in essence is how this assistance program as set out is intended to operate. It is too little and too late. The great mortgage renewal crunch came in August of 1981. What does this government propose to do? It proposes to exclude those home owners by limiting the application of this assistance program to home owners renewing their mortgages between September 1, 1981 and November 11, 1982. In addition, this program is sufficiently mired in red tape that it is expected to assist only 50,000 home owners out of a total of
920,000	home owners who will have to renew their mortgages over the course of the program's short existence. That represents about 5 per cent of the total.
Let us not forget the home owner with equity. The home owner with equity is not receiving assistance as such but merely a deferral of his problem. Sooner or later that home owner will have to pay the bill. Out of the 50,000 home owners who will be assisted, 37,500 will receive nothing more than a temporary respite from their dilemma. The other 12,500-or less than 2 per cent of all home owners renewing-are the only ones who will really receive financial or genuine assistance. Twelve thousand five hundred people may sound like many people at first blush, but 1 want to tell hon. members that following the presentation of the budget an assessment was made in the city of St. Catharines, and it was determined that of a population of 125,000 people, not more than 15 home owners would likely qualify for this assistance. The odds are somewhat better than the odds in a lottery, but they are not something of which the government can be proud. Let us not forget that the majority of home owners who will be renewing their mortgages will be doing so without assistance and without interest deferral.
1 have been impressed by the number of home owners in my home town and across the country who are making financial sacrifices to maintain their homes. The social and economic cost is incalculable. Entertainment budgets are being cut. Car repairs are being put off. Shoes and clothes have to do for another year. Home renovation plans are being scrapped, and grocery budgets are being pared to the bare minimum. More and more we will see home owners looking on their houses as onerous financial burdens they cannot sell and cannot manage or, if they can manage, are barely doing so. The dream of home ownership and the pride of home ownership we had in years gone by was part of a way of life in this country, but it is becoming a nightmare, all because of this government's insane high interest rate policy and this government's broken election promise to hard-pressed home owners.

February 8, 1982
Housing
We in this party are often taunted by the government and by the press for having followed a high interest rate policy ourselves during that Conservative interlude. The current Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) was so concerned about the damaging effects of that policy that he vowed to resign if interest rates exceeded 14 per cent under a Liberal government.
He is still around.

Yes, we did follow a high interest rate policy but, unlike the present government and the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, we honoured our election commitments. We told home owners that there would be high interest rates, but let us not forget that interest rates at that time were 12 per cent and 14 per cent. Our policy was that high interest rates would not be permitted to destroy the market or the joy of continuing home ownership. We provided meaningful relief in the form of a mortgage interest and property tax deductibility program. For 1982 that program would have reduced the effective interest rate on an average $40,000 mortgage calculated at 18 per cent to 13.5 per cent. That is what we on this side of the House call assistance to home owners. Unlike the proposal put forward in the disastrous November 12 budget, our assistance program would have helped every home owner and not just 2 per cent of those renewing or those faced with the renewal of mortgages.
One wag told me that the difference between the Progressive Conservative policy and that of the Liberal Party was the difference between renting and owning. The sad part of it is that the government is not promoting rental policies as an effective alternative. Bill C-89 was written at a time when CMHC itself was predicting a zero vacancy rate by 1983, a black market in rental accommodation and a critical slowdown in rental unit construction. Still, Bill C-89 was written, and since it was written, CMHC forecasts indicate that a zero vacancy rate could be reached as early as this summer. In fact, in many communities across this country that rate has already been reached.
In view of the impending rental crisis, what is this government prepared to do? It says the first step was announced on November 12, and that first step was to slash any private sector incentive to provide the necessary construction of rental units. Soft cost write-offs were eliminated. The multiple unit residential building tax shelter was scrapped and, in return, the government offered interest-free loans of up to $7,500 per unit. The net effect of all that was to say goodbye to some $1 billion worth of new construction in return for $30 million in new tax revenue. Even the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEac-hen)-and he indeed has a checkered record in doing his arithmetic-could see that this was not a particularly good deal for Canada. Accordingly, the minister reinstated the soft cost deduction and the MURB program for just a little while longer, thus putting off real disaster for a little while longer.
What of that $7,500 in rental construction assistance? Builders estimate that this assistance program will give rise to
15,000	starts, or 10,000 fewer starts than was the case last
year under the MURB program. For the government's part, it is assisting the rental crisis by reducing its commitment to social housing by 5,000 units this year. The two programs combined will result in 15,000 fewer places for Canadians to live.
Further, when attempting to project housing and apartment construction starts, we cannot as yet assess the impact of some additional sections contained within the budget proposals. I refer, of course, to the taxation of capital gains on the disposition of an asset, the reduction of the capital cost allowance and those measures which have the effect of reducing people's incentive to save. Savings represent a supply of mortgage funds. By taxing a capital gain at the time of a sale and not when cash is received, the government is in effect demanding a substantially higher down payment for, to pay the tax, the vendor has to get the money to do so. Not only is this tax measure patently unfair and inequitable, but it will also place home ownership further and further away from the ordinary Canadian.
Contrary to what the minister says, the amendments contained in this bill do not provide the flexibility necessary to make it easier for Canadians to acquire homes because under this program there is no way a large number of potential home owners will come close to being able to pay the price. Capital cost allowances, that this government once boasted were the best in the world, have been reduced by half and are bound to drive up housing costs. The builder, especially the landlord constructing new rental accommodation, is already hard pressed to provide affordable living quarters, and this additional cost will not and cannot be absorbed; it must be passed on to the consumer, the potential home occupier. In these times of ever and widely fluctuating interest rates, those with money to invest are less and less attracted to mortgages. Why would anyone want to invest in a mortgage when the interest rate may be five points higher next month? Short-term investments are the preferred choice of many. Anyone looking at the market can see. The stability of mortgage funds supply was being maintained through people's savings, and now even that source of mortgage funds through insurance corporations is being threatened by the November 12 budget.
Canadians, ordinary working Canadians, are discouraged from purchasing their own registered retirement savings plans, as one can no longer claim the interest paid on moneys borrowed for that purpose. Life insurance policies are being attacked as tax loopholes, and this will discourage the purchasing of permanent policies, the kind of policy that provided the source for insurance loan money.
Mr. Speaker, against this backdrop of doom and gloom, the rental and home ownership assistance offered in this Bill C-89 is woefully inadequate. There can be no question that a crisis is looming, and yet we see the federal government sitting idly by, neither caring nor acting. And the minister urges action. Renewing a mortgage today is a nightmare. Trying to find decent, affordable rental accommodation is like trying to find
February 8, 1982

a needle in the proverbial haystack; and trying to make a living in the construction business is even worse than that, it is well nigh impossible. To this list must be added another segment of our society-that I have not yet referred to in any length or detail-which is potentially the hardest hit of all. I might add that the implications to Canada and for Canada are far reaching. What the government is doing is allowing the housing crisis to continue and, by keeping mortgage rates out of sight, is spawning a whole generation of Canadians who no longer believe in the dream of home ownership. They talk in terms of public housing. Our young people have been particularly hard hit by unemployment and are also barely able to make ends meet while living in rented accommodation. They see their parents scrambling to pay the taxes, to meet the mortgage payments, to keep their homes going and to keep food on the table. They see this and they vow that they will not let it happen to them, that they will not be caught in the same position. A house is not a dream or a goal for them to strive for. It is an in and out nightmare that is driving their parents to the wall. They say "Thank you very much, we will avoid that government trap, we will find housing or demand that housing be made available to us from public sources."
Those young people are not deterred by the problem of the marketplace. To purchase an average price home, and the figures were quoted earlier today, to purchase an average price house in Halifax requires a family income of $35,700; in Montreal it is $36,000; and from there you can only go upwards. That is the average cost to acquire a home. But the average household income in Canada is only $27,000. Therefore, even if our average young Canadian family did want to buy a home, the cost of doing so would be prohibitive to him. The end result is that home ownership, the right to hold and own property, is dropped as an objective by this new generation. No longer will we be a nation of home owners. To many it will just be a dream, if they happen to have that kind of dream. What a future, what a futile future for this great country of plenty!
Mr. Speaker, are we, a country of vast geographic expanse, to become a nation of apartment dwellers, a nation where only the rich might own and live in a home, a house of the kind we are used to in this modern day? Is this the goal that brought our forebears to this great country of ours? I would say, surely not. Surely we have been raised to believe in this country and in its promise, and surely one of those promises is that there is an opportunity here to own a piece of land and to build a house upon it. That was my belief and it means as well that it is my desire that this kind of promise in this country be continued.
Hear, hear!

Bill C-89 is not in keeping with this philosophy, as it is the product of a worn out, cynical and indifferent government that has lost the courage, the vision and the wisdom to stand up for Canadians. I can understand the discomfiture of the minister who sponsored this bill today. But, if he does not want to preside over the destruction of the
Housing
Canadian housing industry or the shattering of that Canadian dream, he should resign, and he is honour bound to resign, and thus highlight the housing crisis which he finds himself in; and he must give an opportunity for a new and fresh beginning. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Peterson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak on this important bill about housing. Before commencing my remarks, I cannot avoid making a response to the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid). I listened very carefully to his words this evening. I felt that he was offering us two solutions to the housing problem. Let us all agree that in the ideal world we would want every Canadian to own his own detached, single family dwelling. We would like to see that. Unfortunately, we are not living in a utopian world. We have harsh realities which affect every one of us and which call upon all of us to exercise, at certain times in our economic history, a period of restraint.
I believe that even the members opposite, even those who are slightly noisy in the back rows, agree that we cannot promise everyone everything, even though we would like to see them have it.
What were the two solutions put forward by the hon. member for St. Catharines to the housing problem? Mr. Speaker, the key of his speech was en recherche du temps passe. He presented to us two solutions. Number one was to get rid of our high interest rates. But did he tell us one concrete way we could get rid of those high interest rates? No. He said it would be desirable, that we should get rid of them. Well, that is marvellous, but we know the implications of irresponsible actions, as much as we would like to see high interest rates go down. He did not tell us, if we drove them down below the United States rates, whether his party would be interested in implementing international exchange controls here, in order to keep the money here. He did not tell us about the implications, as to whether he wanted that or not. He, as a matter of fact, condemned the hon. leader of the New Democratic Party when those suggestions were put forward from that quarter. He has not offered us a responsible alternative in any of the measures he suggested, although we would all like to see lower interest rates at this time.
He criticized us, en recherche du temps passe, for getting rid of MURBs. Need I remind hon. members opposite that in their "Clark-Crosbie" budget they First did away with MURBs? It hardly lies within them, when they made a pretence of the integrity of their budget, having told the people what it was, to now rise and criticize us for abolishing MURBs. Perhaps they have reconsidered and believe that MURBs would be a good instrument for getting housing going. But I say that many new foundations have been laid under the MURB program which was extended to December 31 in order to provide rental housing. It has been shown in the past to have been a very effective instrument. If hon. members

February 8, 1982
Housing
opposite are in favour of the MURB program, I should like to see them rise and say it directly rather than wallow in rhetoric without recognizing that it was their party which first abolished the MURB program.
Another possible solution was toyed with by the hon. member for St. Catharines, the solution of mortgage interest deductibility. He said it would be a solution to high housing and mortgage costs. Under their program, mortgage interest deductibility would apply to a limited extent but essentially in an unfair manner. I reject this alternative which would have given the biggest break to the richest taxpayers.
Untrue!
They do not have mortgages on their homes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: A deductibility program for any type of expense always benefits higher-bracket income tax payers more than the lower ones; there is no way to refute it. If that is the hon. member's concept of social justice, if that is a Tory alternative to the government's housing program, it hardly entitles them to damn the positive specific programs outlined in Bill C-89.
Name one.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: I wish to proceed with an enunciation of those particular programs. In summary, the bill enables the Canada mortgage renewal plan to succeed. Also it allows the Canada rental supply plan to operate. It contains provisions for home owners, especially first time ones, and finally, it will enable CMHC to conduct its activities in a more efficient and more responsive manner, considering the difficult financial complexities we now see in Canada's capital markets.
Put them more in debt; that is what you are doing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
I hear the hon. member opposite. Their programs are the ones which ignore restraint and give universal help, across the board, to everyone. This demonstrates more than ever that a Tory is a person who looks forward with optimism to the nineteenth century!
As the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) said, the bill does not represent the government's full agenda for housing concerns. It provides a framework within which we will be able to achieve our full agenda. It provides for very important needs and is necessary for the government to deal effectively with housing issues. It is important to all participants in the housing market-home owners, prospective home owners, developers of rental accommodation, renters, builders and lending institutions.
While there are a number of ways to assess the importance of the bill, perhaps the most direct one is to list briefly what I consider to be the housing problems facing the country at this time and to show how the bill is relevant in meeting those concerns. I believe hon. members on all sides of the House share the first concern, that is the uncertainty facing home
owners because of mortgage renewals when rates are in a great state of flux. There is no doubt that the vast majority of the estimated 635,000 householders expected to renew mortgages this year have the financial capacity to do so, without undue burden on household income, because of the large amount of equity they have in their homes at this time. This equity, or their other resources, will enable many of them to meet the problem of renewing their mortgages because they will have adequate cash flow. Nevertheless, the most important aspect of the bill is that it addresses itself to those people who face real difficulty-those people who cannot renew because of higher interest rates and would be in a position where they might lose their homes, households where families are required to use more than 30 per cent of their income to pay principal, interest and taxes. Primarily the bill addresses itself to those people in need.
We would like to give more money to every home owner, we would like to make every renter a home owner overnight, but in times of restraint ours is a responsible approach to meeting the needs of particular individuals.
This is why we must look at a few facts of the situation. The Canada mortgage renewal plan recognized that home owners have signifcantly higher incomes than renters-$28,000 on average for an owner as against $17,000 for renters. Also home owners have much greater wealth with $72,000 in assets, versus $9,000 for renters. Householders renewing three-year or five-year mortgage plans have generally experienced significant increases in their equity over the past few years. Therefore, a general and high cost program of mortgage renewal assistance, as has been argued by hon. members opposite, would simply be a transfer of income and would not meet the real needs. As we go into tough days ahead, we will have to address the particular needs of those citizens in the country in many of our programs. We will have to reassess the advisability of universal programs. This is one reason our approach to helping home owners with renewal problems, those in the greatest difficulty, is a responsible one in that it meets the most important problems at this particular time of restraint.
There are many other things I should like to say, but I reiterate that at this time we are simply starting our housing program-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
When the House rose at 6 p.m. this evening, I believe the hon. member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson), who had the floor, had completed his remarks. In any event, I do not see him here in the House and
February 8, 1982

accordingly the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Wright) can have the floor.

Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening to speak on Bill C-89, an act to amend the National Housing Act and the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act. In summary this act is to provide legislative authority for the mortgage interest deferral plan outlined in the budget. It is also to provide legislative authority for interest-free loans up to $7,500 per unit per landlord constructing new buildings. It is also to provide an expansion of the types of lending arrangements.
Initially, I would like to refer to a number of statements that have been made in the House by three cabinet ministers. First,
I refer to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) who said on December 10, 1981, referring to the housing crisis in Canada, that this is not the worst crisis we have had. I do not think anyone wants to question whether or not it is the worst housing crisis, but to most people who have outstanding mortgages on their homes it is by far and away the worst that they have ever seen.
Next I want to refer to statements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). On December 3, while in Toronto, the Prime Minister stated that the blame for high interest rates lies with the banks, the market economy and individuals who want good returns on Canada Savings Bonds, and not with his government. If that is not bad enough, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in his budget of November 12, 1981, stated, in part, that we can only expect a decline in interest rates of 1 per cent per year over the next four years. That is not very encouraging for Canadians. In fact, to most Canadians who are attempting to buy homes or who are renewing mortgages, it is close to being a disaster.
I now want to refer to a statement made in the House before dinner this evening. The hon. member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) referred to high interest rates in Canada. He wondered what suggestions we have. I asked him to come back this evening so that I could tell him what suggestions we have. Unfortunately, he has not yet returned to the House. But we must ask ourselves why we have high interest rates. Why are high interest rates causing Canadians so many problems? There must be a reason. Bill C-89 deals with the symptoms but not the disease.
Let us look briefly at why we have high interest rates. The Minister of Finance would like us all to know and believe that we have high interest rates because of our high inflation, and that we must keep interest rates high in order to bring down inflation. Unfortunately, that is not the real reason. I would ask those members opposite who are interested to examine the balance of national payments in Canada for the past year. If they do that, the reason will become apparent to them. The government cannot lower interest rates because of its policies. If it did, it would bring about a monetary crisis in Canada. It recognizes that. Let me spell out very quickly why this is so.
Housing
If one examines the national account balances, one sees that over the past two years $17 billion in long-term capital has left Canada. Now we have been able to bring capital back. In fact, the figure comes to approximately $16 billion which has returned to Canada. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, most of that has been short term. The investment industry calls it hot money. It follows high interest rates. If interest rates are higher here than in other countries, it will flow in; if lower, it will flow out.
So the government's policies discourage long-term capital. This is not speculation, there is no question the figures are there for everyone to see. We have had an exodus of capital and that is so because our world credit rating is not as high as that of some other nations, namely, the United States. That is a fact. Normally our rates should be at least 1 per cent or 2 per cent higher than in the United States in order to encourage long-term capital. So the government's policies have led to this problem.
However, they have another problem. If government has a large deficit, then its demand for capital leads to higher interest rates. 1 do not think anyone will dispute that. We must remember that 50 per cent of all borrowing in Canada today is done by federal and provincial governments.
Another major problem is the defence of the dollar. Provincial governments, with a higher credit rating than Canadian corporations, can borrow money in the United States or Europe cheaper than they can here. That, in turn helps to support the dollar. One has only to look at the amount of borrowing abroad by the provinces to see that is so. This was a policy that the government persuaded the provinces to enact in 1975 or 1976. There was a huge bulge of borrowing by the provinces which has continued to this day. Those are the reasons we have high interest rates. It has little to do with inflation, that is a minor factor. The reason for the outflow of capital is that basically this government has discouraged investment in Canada. The national accounts figures show an exodus of long-term capital.
The other factor, of course, is the government's efforts to nationalize energy companies at a time when they were becoming more Canadian. The government felt it was a good opportunity to step in and buy Canadian companies. If not Canadian-owned, they at best were operated in Canada as good corporate citizens, managed by Canadians. The government decided it wants to own a bigger part of the energy industry. The hon. member for Willowdale says he does not like high interest rates, but he would like to see them lowered; he says the Conservatives do not have any answers.
First of all we have to define the problem. I think I have defined the problem. The question is: what can we do about it? Can we lower interest rates? Yes, but there are certain things we must do, such as encourage exports.
Of course, the hon. member for Willowdale would ask: what exports? We have a surplus of goods that we are not selling abroad, such as natural gas from western Canada. Quite

February 8, 1982
Housing
frankly, if that surplus were in Ontario or in Quebec it would be exported, but because it is in western Canada, the government decided it does not want to do anything else to help western Canada. That is the only reason why our suplus gas is not being exported. The amount of gas available for export has been estimated by provincial governments as approximately $2 billion worth each year. That would be money flowing into this country. We could allow the dollar to float and it would decline, but if we encouraged exports it would not decline that much. And if it did, it would make our manufacturing industries more competitive as they obviously are not at the present time. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association will admit that they are not as competitive as they would like to be. We must encourage long-term, not short-term capital. However, this government would have to do a complete reversal on policy.
What we need, what everyone in Canada has asked for, is a new budget because this one does not address today's problems. It was drawn up a year ago. Thirty Liberal MPs met with the Minister of Finance last fall to tell him it was not a good budget. Ten Liberal MPs wrote a letter to the minister just recently. We could allow our interest rates, Mr. Speaker, to drop by 3 per cent or 4 per cent and it would not harm our dollar that much. It would not drop below 78 cents to 79 cents.
I would now like to come to the housing market. We have to deal with it piecemeal because the government refuses to recognize why we have high interest rates. In the spring of 1980 Calgary had a vacancy rate of 1 per cent, and it is now 0.2 per cent because construction has fallen off. In many parts of Canada, including Alberta, there is a vacancy rate of zero. In effect, there are no vacancies. At the present time, the cost of the average home in Calgary is $111,000. I am referring to the average home. One must make an income of $62,000 just to afford a home in Calgary. The average mortgage is $50,000. The average Canadian cannot afford that.
During the last three years, the average increase in interest cost per year for a home has been between $2,000 and $3,000. That is absolutely ridiculous. It is not due to the mortgage companies and it is not due to the banks; it is due to the interest rates brought in by this government and carried out by the Bank of Canada. In Canada at this time, we need an average of 220,000 homes or units constructed each year; however, according to the Conference Board, 180,000 may be constructed next year, resulting in a shortfall of 40,000 units. The outlook for the next two years is no better. We will have a shortfall of over 100,000 units over the next two to three years, and this government is not addressing the problem. What is the government suggesting? It is suggesting that it will bring in a plan to assist the renters and home owners. What is this plan? This two-year plan would have a capital requirement of $350 million spent over two years, of which $150 million would be spent this year, and $200 million spent next year.
What does it actually mean when one breaks it down? It means that the government will provide a subsidy to lenders to
build up to 15,000 rental units at $7,500 per unit. The government will provide rental assistance for 15,000 units in Canada when there is a need for 100,000 units. The government has hardly scratched the surface of the problem.
What rental units will this help? The average break-even cost for a lender in rental units today is $800. When a lender constructs an apartment block, he must receive a rent of $800 per unit in order to break even. The average subsidized housing in Canada has a rental cost of $400 per month. That means that if one lives in subsidized housing, one pays an average of $400 a month. The average cost is $800 for all other people in Canada.
What will the government do? It will provide a benefit to the lenders to construct rental apartments for those in the higher rental brackets, not those in the lower brackets. Once again, people in lower income tax brackets will be left out because no lender will build subsidized homes unless forced. How does one force them to build for the lower rental market? One cannot.
Therefore, if we look at the $150 million subsidy the government will provide, we find that 15,000 units times $7,500 amounts to $112 million which the government will provide for rental housing. Out of $150 million, the government will have $38 million left over to assist those who are in dire straits as a result of their mortgage renewals. Obviously, this will not help them If one is renewing a mortgage, and 30 per cent of one's gross income is less than one's principal and interest, one may apply for a loan guarantee. If one's equity in one's home is less than five per cent, the government may allow a one-time grant of $3,000. However, one must have renewed one's mortgage between September 1, 1981, and November 12, 1982.
It does not appear that this will do very many people any good. Surely most people who have owned a home for three to five years would have more than five per cent equity in their homes. Obviously, this offers nothing for most people. If one calculates this benefit, one finds that the maximum number of people who will be helped by this loan or guarantee or loan grant will be 15,000. However, 1,200,000 people will renew mortgages over the next two years. Where is the help the minister promised? It is not there.
Let us look at the MURB program, which is of benefit only when interest rates are high. It was not of much benefit, as the builders will tell us, at lower interest rates, those below 13 per cent or 14 per cent. However, at interest rates above 16 per cent to 18 per cent, the MURBs become very attractive.
Go to Whistler!

What has the government stated? It has stated that it will eliminate the MURB program. Concerning rental units, whereas the government is now providing subsidies for
25.000	rental units, it will reduce that to 15,000 units, amounting to a reduction of 10,000 units per year. Concerning subsidized housing, the government will reduce the subsidy from the former 30,000 down to 25,000, amounting to a reduction of 5,000 units. That amounts to a total reduction of
15.000	units over the next year. What does the construction

industry state? It states that for every unit built, whether a rental unit or a home, it takes one and a half construction workers to build that unit, on the average. That means that there will be 15,000 fewer units, multiplied by the one and a half employees who would have built those units. That means we will have an increase in unemployment of 22,500 over the next year. Where is the justice in that? The government really does not know how to solve the problem. All it can do is to create more unemployment as a result of this bill.
If we look at the mobility of labour in Canada, we find that as a result of the high interest rates, the high cost of rental units and the high cost of homes, people are unwilling to move from one part of Canada to another because it is too expensive. They may decide they should stay in an area of high unemployment and receive unemployment benefits or welfare benefits rather than move to a high employment area. Where is the justice in that? Why would a government bring out a budget and a bill such as this which would encourage unemployment?
People within the mortgage market recently told the government that, for all intent and purposes, the mortgage market in Canada has dried up. If one asks the Minister of Public Works in the House, he will deny that. He will say we still have an active mortgage market, but the average Canadian is no longer involved in buying a home. He cannot afford it. Many Canadians cannot afford $800 a month in rent, but still this government wishes to continue with its high interest policy.
Why has the mortgagee market dried up? It is because the government brought out Canada Savings Bonds last fall by which it raised $19.5 billion. It took much potential money out of the mortgage market and put it into savings where it will remain for one to two years. By increasing interest rates, other lenders who would have put their money into mortgages, put it into short-term investment in order to obtain a better return. That is why the mortgage industry has been saying the mortgage market has dried up.
What about the life insurance companies which are noted for providing long-term mortgages? Even during the last couple of years, a period of high interest rates and short-term investments, they have been providing 15, 20 and 25-year mortgages, but the government does not tell you that. What does it do? It virtually cancelled income annuities.
In Alberta there would be no homes or apartments built if it were not for Alberta Housing. That is the only reason the people of Alberta are now able to buy or rent new accommodation. That comes from the Alberta Heritage Fund. For those who wonder about the Alberta Heritage Fund, it was that fund which protected Albertans from the scarcity of housing that has occurred in other parts of Canada.
This minister has not given us anything that we really want or need or that will help the people of Canada. We are going to be very interested in discussing some of these questions with the minister in committee. Bill C-89 does not address the
Housing
problem. The housing industry in its desperation is saying, "We don't like it, but it is better than nothing. If we cannot have it all, give us a little piece. If we cannot have lower rates and fairness in the mortgage markets, we will accept this little bit." They will have to come back to the government in six months or a year and ask whether there is something else that can be done for them. The government may think about it. It may give them another little bit to help the mortgage market, but far less than it should. However, it will at least help it.
We are going to examine this bill in committee very carefully and find out why this minister goes along with high interest rates, why he is not prepared to help those Canadians in desperate need of accommodation and why he has provided nothing but a drop in the bucket. The Minister of Public Works is the minister of a drop in the bucket.

Mr. Speaker, in my remarks in support of Bill C-89, an act to amend the National Housing Act and the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act, I will be concentrating on the mortgage insurance fund and the two major social housing programs that have had a considerable impact on the financial status of that fund. To put my comments in the proper perspective 1 want to make a few general remarks about the housing situation in Canada today.
There have always been persons inadequately housed, even in 1982. I understand that about 2 per cent of the houses in this country are still without modern conveniences. Nevertheless, during the last decade, housing starts in Canada averaged over 230,000 units per annum. Compare that to the United States, the prosperous country to the south, where during the same decade housing starts averaged 1.77 million per annum. Thus, on a per capita basis we were building housing in Canada at a rate more than 30 per cent greater than in the United States.
Because I am from the construction industry, have experience in all provinces and have visited many of the states, I am prepared to add that our standards of quality are generally superior to those in the United States. I give full credit for that exceptional performance to the Canada Housing and Mortgage Corporation. Their success has been in spite of the provincial governments and with no thanks to the Constitution which leaves the major responsibility for construction activity under provincial control.
1 was angry last week when 1 watched the federal-provincial conference of first ministers. The provinces restrain, hinder and impede and still come with their hands out for more money. How many people in Quebec know that the federal government shares with the provincial government the cost of rent subsidies, that it shares the cost of deficits and provides financing or the guarantee of financing for up to 90 per cent, 95 per cent and even 100 per cent for rental accommodation for which the provincial government tries to take all the credit?
In 1980 CMHC contributed over $9 million in operating grants in Quebec and $34 million in contributions to deficits. The housing critic for the Official Opposition received a response to a question on January 27 last indicating that as at

February 8, 1982
Housing
December 31, 1980, there were 148,336 units under the administration of the NHA that were provincially-owned rentals, CMHC-financed. That same answer to the question of the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) indicated that CMHC, through the mortgage insurance fund, had, on September 30, 1981, 9,538 vacant housing units of which 1,882 were acknowledged to be in areas where there was no demand. That left 7,656 units available for occupancy. I would like to read the following paragraph from the 1980 annual report of CMHC:
By the beginning of 1980, the federal government, through CMHC, was committed to providing operating subsidies on a long-term basis for 225,000 dwelling units. For 1980 it authorized CMHC to make commitments for a further 26,750 dwelling units. During the year, however, approval was given for commitments for an additional 5,000 new dwelling units, to help alleviate very tight rental markets in such cities as Vancouver, Calgary and Toronto.
That means that total NHA social housing subsidy commitments exceed a quarter million units. This country can be very proud of the contribution that the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation has made in providing the financing or the guarantee of financing that has helped and is helping so many millions of Canadians.
I want to turn now to the subject of the mortgage insurance fund. In 1978, the assets of the mortgage insurance fund decreased for the first time since it was established in 1954. There was a further decrease in the fund in the year 1980 from $512 million at the beginning of the year to $314 million at year end. Mortgage loan insurance was introduced in 1954 when the National Housing Act was amended to permit the chartered banks to enter into the residential lending field. By protecting the lenders against the risk of loss, NHA mortgage insurance encouraged approved lenders to invest in mortgages. Mortgage insurance fees paid to CMHC by brokers are accumulated in a mortgage insurance reserve fund. Lenders may claim against the fund in the event that a borrower defaults on his payments and a foreclosure results.
Over 40 per cent of the five million dwellings completed since 1954 have been insured by CMHC. Over $50 billion in capital funds has been attracted toward investment in housing since the amendment to the National Housing Act over 25 years ago.
A letter which I received from the minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing dated October 22, 1980, signed by the minister himself, stated:
I agree that it would be inequitable for CMHC to raise its mortgage insurance premiums to recover the losses incurred in insuring loans under the Assisted Home Ownership Program and the Assisted Rental Program.
As you point out in your letter, these were social programs and accordingly, their social cost should not be borne by those seeking National Housing Act mortgage insurance, but by the government.
Mr. Speaker, no provision was made at that time for these programs which were introduced then, with the result that the mortgage insurance fund has borne this risk and is now bearing the cost.
I have read this excerpt from the letter of the minister because at that time I heard rumours that there may be an increase in the percentage which was to be charged by CMHC and, as everyone knows, at one time the amount in the mortgage insurance fund exceeded $600 million. 1 was most anxious to ensure that if we were going to introduce social housing programs to use up these available funds, the cost should not be borne by those who had taken out regular mortgages.
In the mid-1970s, the mortgage insurance fund reserve was in excess of $600 million. This was several hundred million more than all the expected liabilities. The government used this excess to underwrite two social housing programs; the Assisted Home Ownership Program known as AHOP and the Assisted Rental Program known as ARP. These programs were designed to make home ownership available to more people and to put more rental units into tight markets. Well over 200,000 units were constructed under these programs.
Until now, the cost of initiating mortgage insurance business was borne by the corporation, for which it received an application fee. This fee originally was $35 and was increased to $100 last year. It never has been adequate to cover the associated costs. The costs not charged to the mortgage insurance fund are estimated to be approximately $75 million. The reason I mention this figure is to keep all the costs which have been charged to the mortgage insurance fund in perspective.
The cost of business initiation included the receiving and reviewing of applications, the receipt and posting of fees and insurance premiums, recording of insurance policy information in the corporation's files and computing systems and the carrying out of inspections and appraisals. These inspections ensure compliance with housing standards.
I would like to make a few remarks about the inspection process since I feel that it is relevant. I was always somewhat intrigued by the fact that CMHC was insuring mortgages and that most people were able to get somewhat preferential rates from the bank or lending institution if the mortgage was insured by CMHC. Why, then, would there be any private company in business in apparent competition with CMHC? One of the reasons concerns inspections.
Being in the construction industry, 1 wanted to find out for myself. I travelled across the country and visited several construction sites where contractors whom I knew were working with the company in the private sector which was insuring mortgages. In almost all cases there was no doubt that the consumer, or occupant of the house, would generally be paying about one half per cent more in the final analysis. The builder was expressing dissatisfaction with the inspection practices of CMHC. In fact, it was not so much the inspection practices which were at fault as the fact that the standard being imposed upon the construction by CMHC inspectors was higher than the standard being imposed by the private sector. Not only was the home owner being protected, he was also obtaining the benefit of a slightly lower interest rate on his house.
February 8, 1982

Nevertheless, this company continued to operate. Of course, the company is the Mortgage Insurance Company of Canada. Just last month, on January 19, I read that one of the developments in the history of this company was its merger with the only other private sector mortgage insurer in Canada, Insmor Holdings Ltd. of Toronto.
1 make the point now that, apart from this one organization, there is only Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to turn to if we want to be sure that the consumer has the protection of the government. The claim was made that the merged companies can better compete against the other source of mortgage insurance, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I found it interesting that in the same article there was a comment attributed to William Mulholland, Chairman of the Bank of Montreal, who said that the number of mortgages in arrears by three months or more dropped by 15 per cent between June, 1980 and June, 1981, despite a 5 per cent increase in interest rates during that period. These two items are not particularly tied together but they happen to appear in the same article, and 1 thought that the second comment by the Chairman of the Bank of Montreal was worth recording here.
I will take a few moments to put on the record the present status of the mortgage insurance fund. As at November 30 last year, the fund assets were as follows: mortgage assets, that is mortgages held by the fund, totalled $124 million; real estate assets, these real estate assets are at market value, totalled $424 million. For those interested in the book value-the acquisition price-the figure is $523 million. This loss is included in the loss figures which are to be mentioned in connection with this particular program.
The fund had $24 million in other assets. The current deficit in the fund is $339.3 million. That is made up of a debt to CMHC of $56 million and a debt to the Government of Canada of $283.6 million.
The total assets as at November 30 were $232 million. Incidentally, the fund receives approximately $30 million per annum in premiums. An actuarial study suggests the fund is deficient by about $210 million.
Bill C-89 is intended to assist in putting the mortgage insurance fund back on a sound financial basis. I should interject, as 1 talk about AHOP and ARP, to say that the rundown of the amount in the mortgage insurance fund is almost entirely attributable to these two programs which were introduced as social housing programs and which, for reasons 1 shall be explaining, resulted in a depletion of the cash, the amount of which at one time exceeded $600 million.
The provisions relating to the underwriting of loan insurance are largely of an administrative nature. A significant change is the new section proposed by the bill by which the corporation is given the authority to determine the insurance premium in relation to an approved loan, the premium to be in such amount as the corporation considers appropriate in view of the
Housing
risks entailed and the costs and expenses incurred by the corporation in relation to the insurance. Each line of business is to be analysed actuarially with a view to establishing and quantifying the risk posed by that line of business. Such an analysis will consider, among other things, historical foreclosure rates, borrower's capacity to repay and the expected economic climate during the risky part of the mortgage life. This analysis will enable the fund to strike a suitable premium for each business line. With such an arrangement, the fund can serve the government's social purposes but with a knowledge of the total financial implications of each program. This will allow full consideration of the total costs of the proposed program.
I must interject that if we had known the costs of the two programs, AHOP and ARP, perhaps we might not have proceeded, or we might not have proceeded to the extent we did and, in my opinion, Canada would have been the poorer for that.
Once this legislation is passed, the old and new funds will be kept separately on the corporation's books so that the problems of the past do not drag the newly instituted fund into financial disarray. The new fund can be monitored and premiums adjusted according to changes in programs.
I want to spend a few minutes discussing the two major social housing programs which are the principal reason why the cash in the mortgage insurance fund has been so depleted. Under the Assisted Home Ownership Program total claims to date come to $515 million. The accumulated loss to date totals $230 million, and this includes known future losses not yet incurred. Actuaries calculate that 4 per cent of insured value would be the fee necessary to cover risk, and 1 have no hesitation in suggesting that it would be pointless to introduce a program such as AHOP and at that point to impose on those persons who are to be assisted a fee of 4 per cent.
It should be noted that the program provided for a 5 per cent down payment. That was to be the equity of the purchaser of the home. However, there were some federal grants which reduced the down payment even further, and additionally- always, apparently, working at cross-purposes-provincial grants further reduced the down payment to the point where, with assistance from the builder, it was possible for the occupants of AHOP houses to move in with little or no down payment whatsoever. Thus, the owner of the house-and 1 probably should put "owner" in quotation marks-was occupying premises with little or no down payment at a monthly mortgage repayment figure which was, because of its deferral, less than the normal amount he or she could be expected to pay and, therefore, the owner was in effect able to live for a period of up to five years in what one might term subsidized accommodation.
Some 99,000 units were produced, and of those 99,000 units approximately 13,000 are termed walk-aways; they were occupied and then the owners left, often at the end of the five-year period when mortgages were automatically increased to take care of the lower payments which had been made during the first five years.

I note from the figures that in Quebec-and this information was made available on February 3-some 40,000 units were sold at a total value of $1,148 billion. This compares with 41,500 units in the province of Ontario at a total value of $1,628 billion. It is interesting, when looking at these two figures, to note that in the province of Quebec, where the total number of units sold was approximately the same as in Ontario, there was a total of 1,836 actions taken on AHOP units, that is, acquisitions, for a total of $53 million, whereas in the province of Ontario, with only a few more units built, the number of actions taken, acquisitions, was 8,581 for a total of $318 million. I intend to discuss the reason for the difference in these two figures in Quebec and Ontario; however, it is important to emphasize that the successfully housed rate was over 80 per cent of all the units built.
We should break down the remaining less than 20 per cent. About 13 per cent were the walk-aways to which I referred earlier, the acquisitions, those who did not continue with their houses, and approximately 6.5 per cent or 7 per cent were not even occupied. This makes up the total of about 19.5 per cent, which one might term the failure rate. However, let us bear in mind that among that 13 per cent I have been talking about there were many people who enjoyed living in houses for periods of up to five years, making what was, in effect, subsidized monthly payments with little or no down payments. Thus, approximately seven out of every eight who occupied houses under this program were successfully housed, that is, given the opportunity to own their own homes as the result of the introduction of this program.
An analysis of the market factors behind the high AHOP default experience is appropriate. AHOP claims are primarily from Ontario and British Columbia. In fact, 77 per cent of the
9.000	AHOP units acquired by the mortgage insurance fund were in those two provinces. The ratio of mortgage insurance fund acquisitions compared with approvals in Quebec is only 2.8 per cent, whereas in Ontario the ratio of acquisitions to approvals is 9.7 per cent, and in British Columbia it is 10.5 per cent.
To examine the issue regarding substantial variations in the AHOP default rate between Ontario and Quebec, one needs to look at the types of housing unit produced under the AHOP in the two provinces.
In Quebec, of the 43,000 units, just over 1,000 were condominiums and 42,000 were freehold and other units. However, of the 50,000 in Ontario, 33,000 were condominiums and
17.000	were freehold and other units. Thus, although the default rate in condominiums is approximately the same in Quebec as in Ontario, 10.6 per cent in Quebec and 12.6 per cent in Ontario, because of the lower number of condominiums, when one compares it to the default rate in the freehold and other types, 2.6 per cent in Quebec and 3.8 per cent in Ontario, one can see that while the rate in Quebec is much lower than the rate in Ontario, in fact the rate in Ontario is
more than three times, almost four times, the default rate in the province of Quebec.
These figures reveal a significant difference between the types of dwelling units produced in the two provinces. In Ontario, condominium rows and apartments represented two thirds of the production of AHOP units, whereas in Quebec more than 95 per cent of the AHOP units were single and semi-detached freehold units. The insurance risk is higher for condominium than for freehold units, and it is therefore not surprising that AHOP default rates in Ontario are substantially higher than in Quebec.
The second social housing program which has impacted heavily on the mortgage insurance fund is the assisted rental program where the accumulated losses totalled $186 million, and most of this loss has been and is being incurred in Montreal.
Actuaries calculate that 8 per cent of insured value would be the fee necessary to cover risk. Under this program, 123,000 units of rental housing were produced; and 1 think it would be abundantly apparent to everyone that if 8 per cent had been added to the cost of the mortgage in order to cover the actuarially calculated risk factor, there would have been very few of those 123,000 units produced. To assess the consequences of the impact of the Assisted Rental Program, requires an analysis of the market factors behind the high ARP default experience. As of March 31, 1980, 78.3 per cent of the 6,741 ARP units acquired by the mortgage insurance fund were in Quebec. In the first half of the 1970s, the demand for new rental housing in Montreal averaged 18,700 units per year, while only 14,000 units were being supplied per year. As a result, the Montreal rental market experienced increasing tightness. The demand for new rental housing resulted in part from the large expansion of employment in the province. The average annual growth in employment opportunities between 1970 and 1976 was 55,000 jobs.
These favourable economic circumstances were associated with the turnaround in migration patterns. Rather than experiencing a net outward movement of population, the situation was one in which there was an actual net population gain between June 1974 and May 1975. The tremendous demand pressure pushed rental vacancy rates down from 8.2 per cent in 1970 to only 0.6 per cent in April, 1976; and apartment construction in Montreal responded rapidly.
However, economic conditions worsened in Quebec in 1976. Employment growth stagnated, with a net loss of 23,000 jobs in 1977. In addition, after the election of the Parti Quebecois in November, 1976, net outflows of population from Quebec accelerated from 9,600 between June, 1976 and May, 1977, to
54,000	between June, 1977 and May, 1978. It is estimated that the reduction in job creation, coupled with the acceleration of out-migration, translated into a drop in rental demand from an average of 18,700 units per year during the first half of the 1970s, to 8,800 units in 1976, to 4,500 units in 1977 and to 5,200 units in 1978. The upsurge in apartment starts, pushed completions up from 12,500 units in 1976 to 18,600 units in 1977; and vacancy rates in Montreal rose rapidly.

The occupancy rate in new projects was reported to be around 48 per cent; and in April, 1980, the rate fell to 27 per cent.
In 1976, net migration began to increase significantly as economic conditions worsened and because of political developments in the province. Migration flows had a major impact on the assisted rental program default experience. The impact of net migration on foreclosures can be illustrated by these figures. In the province of Quebec, between 1973 and 1976 the net change in the population was an increase of 1,096; in the period from 1976 to 1979 the loss was 103,992.
Mr. Speaker, it is relevant, I think, to read a short extract from a letter dated December 2, 1981, which the Housing and Urban Development Association of Canada sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and members of the federal cabinet. It reads:
Current levels of rent are so out of line with the costs of producing rental accommodation that there is no prospect for easing the vacancy problem without additional incentives or subsidies.
HUDAC, that is, the Housing and Urban Development Association of Canada go on to estimate in the same letter that to put rental housing on a basis that would attract investor participation would require rent increases of 60 per cent or more.
I wanted to read that extract from what is considered the foremost housing association in Canada because of the significance of those Figures when they talk about the need for rent increases of 60 per cent or more in order to attract investor participation.
When one invests in a house, one looks at one's ability to pay the mortgage, it is true, but also one feels that in due course, because of inflation, there is likely to be some appreciation in value; and in fact, for most people in this country, there has been a reasonably good increase in equity over the years. However, with rental accommodation, the value of the property is of little significance. Investors are concerned solely with return on investment.
One of the difficult experiences for the mortgage insurance fund has been the realization that while one can build an apartment complex-and I have an example in my hand of one which is not too far from my constituency-it may cost some $7 million. In this particular case the mortgage was a little more than $6 million. If the owner of a project goes bankrupt because of rental experience and, as a result, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation ends up being the owner of the property, when it comes to sell the project, since it is not the intention of CMHC to stay in the real estate business, the price will be substantially lower than the amount of the mortgage. It has nothing to do with the value of the property from a construction point of view. It is simply because rents are so low that there is an inadequate return on investment. In the case of the purchase of such a property, it is rather like buying a bond-one looks simply at the amount of the cost and the amount of the return.

In looking at the project to which I have referred, I found it interesting that in a period of some 19 years gross revenues exceeded gross expenditures by only $2 million, comparing a little under $13 million of expenditures with a little under $15 million of gross revenues. At the time the project was started, it had a mortgage at 5'/s per cent. It occurred to me to look at what would have been the amount of money one would have received, compounded on the mortgage at that percentage, and it came to something over $5 million. Thus we see a project with construction costs of $7 million, a mortgage of $6 million, but a return which meant that when it was offered for sale it was difficult to obtain a bid of $3 million.

The point I was making was that one must look at the experience of the Assisted Rental Program in the mortgage insurance fund to understand why there was such an apparent loss in what has been an excellent rental as well as an excellent social program. It is an answer to a question which I received on June 17, 1981, wherein the minister responsible for CMHC pointed out that the average time lag from the date of a borrower's default on payments to the time when title is conveyed to CMHC, under the terms of the mortgage loan insurance policy, is 414 calendar days.
