Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on Bill C-89 to amend the National Housing Act and the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act. Housing is a vital industry in Canada, and its continued existence and

February 8, 1982
Housing
growth is fundamental as more and more Canadians require shelter in a shrinking market and face severe economic hardships. Our society is built upon the premise that ownership of private property is an inherent freedom. The erosion of ability to own property is a serious social problem in Canada today. The right to own property guards the troubled boundary between the individual and the state. It is not the only separation as many other traditions, institutions and laws are also important, but Canadians have always taken pride in ownership of property.
There is no question that record high interest rates have done much to harm seriously the housing situation in Canada. The dream of many Canadians to acquire a home of their own has been shattered largely as a result of government economic policies or lack thereof. Two serious housing problems have developed in Canada over the past two years, those being availability and affordability, both largely as a result of high interest rates. When not enough housing units are produced to support the demand, we see shortages in supply. It has been estimated that Canada needs some 220,000 new housing units each year. During 1980, only some 159,000 new units were built, while in 1981, only some 178,000 units were built. The November, 1981, Conference Board forecast predicts that only
180,000	units will be constructed in 1982. These figures indicate a possible shortage of 143,000 units over a three-year period. Investors faced with high interest rates think twice about investing money in construction these days. As a result, apartment construction has virtually ground to a halt. The national vacancy rate fell from 2.8 per cent in April 1980 to some 1.2 per cent in October 1981, and continues to fall. As we have heard in the House this evening, in some areas it is zero. Many large centres across Canada experience serious shortages as more and more people compete with fewer housing unit vacancies. It is not just home owners who are experiencing problems these days, but also renters who are facing a bleak housing market. This will continue unless current adverse trends are turned around.
It is hard to believe that in a country with so much space and so many resources, as well as the over-all potential of a standard of living second to none, there should be any housing problems. It is up to the Government of Canada to implement programs to reduce interest rates for housing in an effort to provide Canadians with an adequate supply of housing units which are basic to the strength of any country. The government should realize it is difficult to ask Canadians to deal with the serious economic issues facing them today, without the added worry of struggling just to keep the basic necessity of a roof over their heads. Canadians must feel confident about the security of their family units and the basics such as food, shelter and clothing, as we tackle the problems of high inflation, interest rates, unemployment and rapidly increasing energy costs.
High mortgage rates are clearly having an impact upon the affordability of housing. In the third quarter of 1981, the average price of a home sold in Canada was $77,900. Assuming a 10 per cent down payment and $1,000 in property taxes.
and using the rule of thumb that total payments for principal, interest and taxes should not exceed 30 per cent of gross income, a family income of $45,000 is now needed to afford an average-priced home. Canadian home owners, or hopeful home owners, have been faced with dramatic price increases due to high interest rates and rising house prices on the market in the last few years, the results of which are being felt today.
According to CMHC, as many as 40,000 Canadian families may lose their homes because of high interest rates. Many of these people are hardworking members of society trying to get ahead but frustrated in their efforts by the poor state of our economy brought about by years of federal government neglect and high interest rate policy. Approximately 1,200,000 Canadian families will have to renew their mortgages over the next two years, many at substantial increases in monthly payments. This will place undue pressure on an already stretched budget. These two problems of availability and affordability of housing units are serious indeed and deserve and demand immediate and effective government action in an effort to set things straight.
Canadians expected relief in the form of responsible solutions to the economic problems facing the country, but have found that relief in the recent federal budget was virtually non-existent. While the budget offers builders some assistance in the construction of new apartments, the limited assistance will only have a slight impact on the high break-even costs faced by most builders.
The MURB program which was responsible for the construction of some 25,000 rental units last year has been cancelled, and the government will reduce its commitment to subsidize social housing in 1982 from 30,000 units to 25,000 units. That is a drop of 5,000 units. The net effect of the above two policy decisions is a reduction of some 15,000 needed housing starts. The government promised, after continuous criticism throughout the summer and early fall, to bring in some form of relief for home owners in dire straits, such as people facing huge mortgage rate increases because of the government's high interest rate policy. The relief brought forward in the budget, if you can call it relief, or for that matter if you can call it a budget, is little more than a program which allows people to keep their homes by going further into debt.
The proposed Canada mortgage renewal plan as contained in Bill C-89 does little, if anything, to resolve Canada's current housing crisis. On an average-priced home in Canada today at the high level of interest being paid on a mortgage spread over the length of a usual repayment period, a Government of Canada guarantee to defer interest or for those who qualify for a grant, the maximum relief of $3,000 is minimal and not an effective solution to such a serious problem. This proposed plan is to expire on November 11, 1982, and apply to mortgages which matured on or after September 1, 1981. Such a short-term measure, which the minister responsible for CMHC indicated "is providing the help people need to get
February 8, 1982

them through these difficult times," must be questioned as to its effectiveness since some three months after the federal budget we see no improvement on the economic and housing horizon. This is not surprising since the so-called budget did not address itself to providing solutions to the causes of our economic and housing woes.
In the information kit on the proposed Canada mortgage renewal plan issued on November 12, 1981, in the questions and answers section, this question is posed: "This proposed plan appears to me to be simply a postponement of the inevitable. I will still face a hardship situation in a year from now when this plan runs out. What do I do then?"
The answer section indicates that the Canadian government "is simply unable to afford an extended benefit plan." Recent reports indicate the federal government is to spend millions of dollars on advertising the new Canadian Constitution, which I am sure will be of small comfort to struggling home owners. The answer goes on as follows:
It is hoped, however, that while the plan is in operation, the personal financial situation of home owners will improve to the point where a decreasing proportion of income will be required to carry monthly mortgage charges. At the same time, this is an opportunity for home owners to consider their personal situations and to plan for the period when the plan terminates.
I would suggest that if the personal financial situation of home owners improves to any degree between now and November 11, 1982, it will not be as a result of any efforts on behalf of the federal government whose three-months-old budget has done little but slam the average Canadian.
I would also suggest, Mr. Speaker, that, at the same time, this is an opportunity for home owners, and indeed for all Canadians, to consider the economic mess in which this government has put the country, and an opportunity to plan to replace this worn out government with a Progressive Conservative government.
Bill C-89, while dealing with provisions of the mortgage interest renewal plan, also deals with various other measures which the government says will make CMHC "more businesslike and more flexible". I would hope that such changes would result in effective and efficient programs and service to the public through fair and effective programs designed to improve the housing situation in Canada.
These are trying times for many Canadians. The 12.5 per cent annual average rate of inflation in 1981 was the largest annual average rate in 33 years. Unbelievable interest rates, record unemployment and energy costs, are changing the lifestyles of many hardworking Canadians through no fault of their own. Luxuries are the first items to go as part of the cost-cutting forced by rapidly increasing costs and more slowly increasing incomes. Canadians can learn to live with temporary reductions in their standard of living if they realize that effective solutions are forthcoming to get the nation's economy on the rails again.
After so many years of economic mismanagement by the present government, the Canadian people are losing their patience. In 1968, Canada's standard of living was the third highest in the western world; by 1981, it was thirteenth. With
Housing
our abundant resources, Canada should have the highest standard of living and be on top. Many hardworking Canadians are finding that these economic hardships are gouging out not just the luxuries of life, but the necessities of life as well. Many Canadians, often families where both the husband and wife work, are finding it difficult to provide food, clothing and shelter for their families. It used to be in Canada that a single breadwinner maintained an increasing standard of living while paying off a mortgage, but now such a concept is but a dream to many Canadians. It is bad enough that many unemployed Canadians are having serious problems maintaining adequate housing, but when working families start losing their homes, the government must realize the seriousness of the problem.
The rural and native housing program, which is administered by CMHC, has caused a great deal of controversy in my riding of Hastings-Frontenac-Lennox and Addington. This program was approved by the federal cabinet in 1974. Its original objectives were to ensure adequate housing for low-income persons living in rural areas and small communities with a population of 2,500 or less. The program encourages client involvement to motivate and help the program's clients solve their housing problems through their own organization and efforts by providing the opportunity for client involvement in the planning and building of the units.
The program operates with various benefits and assistance available to those eligible. Section 40 of the National Housing Act is considered the lead provision under the rural and native housing program. Section 40 is the home ownership part of the program whereby ownership is made possible to low-income families by gearing monthly payments to income in accordance with a purchase-payment-to-income scale. This is a federal-provincial cost-sharing program whereby capital costs and losses are shared on a 72-25 per cent basis. I understand that under this part of the program the houses were to be built or acquired by CMHC and then sold to clients at the subsidized rates.
The program is designed to assist people to purchase a home and to pay for it based on their capacity to pay rather than the housing cost. Payments are based on 25 per cent of income with a minimum down payment of $500-or "sweat equity."
I understand that the program went into operation very quickly after it was approved by cabinet but before adequate guidelines and procedures could be developed, and that in October, 1976, the first formal directives were issued to the field offices, giving decentralized authority to branch managers for rural and native housing under Section 40, resulting in some inconsistencies.
In 1977, because of difficulties encountered in achieving targeted goals for the first few years of the program, a special task force was appointed by CMHC to review the total program, and a number of policy and procedural issues were identified and brought to the attention of management for resolution. In light of recent concerns in my riding over the program, I ask the minister to review policies and procedures

February 8, 1982
Housing
to ensure the smooth and effective working of the rural and native housing program.
In view of the very high interest rates of the last two years, the housing crisis in Canada has deepened beyond certain select groups. People in the cities, towns and on farms are experiencing problems in trying to keep a roof over their heads. Families where both spouses work hard to get ahead are finding it hard to hold on to their houses, if they can even afford one at all. Many who work hard just to hang on to their homes find that many other sacrifices are necessary also.
In light of such troubled times facing so many Canadians, it is necessary that various government programs be not only fair but be seen to be fair and appropriate for the times. Many people who work hard to get ahead and pay their taxes do not feel it is fair when, through no fault of their own, they lose their homes or have to struggle to maintain them, while at the same time the government offers a heavily subsidized program to a chosen few to acquire housing. Such a program, while commendable in principle during sound economic times, is felt by some to be out of tune with today's troubled times. This is not to say there is no need for government programs to aid Canadians' housing problems, but rather that existing programs should be equitable and appropriate.
I understand that under Section 40, CMHC can either purchase existing homes or have new homes built. This would, or perhaps should, entail an adequate selection of sites, builders, or an inventory of houses in a targeted area. Questions arise as to the criteria to be followed, the search process and the best decision for those affected. Questions also arise as to the selection of participants, and here we must remember this program is set up for communities of fewer than 2,500 people where often you find they know each other and what goes on in their community.
There is a controversy in my riding concerning the home ownership aspect of the rural and native housing program, and 1 would like to set out what I perceive to be some problems associated with it, particularly in Madoc and Marmora. When it is decided to go into an area with the program, it is necessary to select the best way to advertise and make the program known to eligible persons. At a time when so many Canadians are experiencing high housing costs and shortages, it is important that any program be adequately made known to avoid controversy and achieve a fair and representative response.
What are the best means of getting the information to and identifying potential applicants? Does CMHC contact local municipalities, welfare, community and social agencies, or federal and provincial Members of Parliament for a possible client list? Is there to be television, radio or newspaper advertising, or public meetings in target areas to acquaint all interested local residents with the program? After all, this is a taxpayer subsidized program for certain people at a time when many other taxpayers are losing their homes and going into debt. It is imperative that suitable guidelines exist to ensure adequate information and feedback.
Then there is the decision on whether to build new or buy existing housing, which raises questions and concerns. Who does CMHC approach to assess local housing and land markets? Should it be local real estate agents, municipal officials, the applicants, local residents or the local media? Are only those houses and lots listed for sale looked into, or is an effort made to find out about additional property which might come on the market? What guidelines exist as to requirements for the housing being sought, and on what basis is the decision made to buy existing or build new homes? I feel these and other issues must be addressed in order to provide comprehensive guidelines for this important program.
There are also areas of concern as to the successful applicants. How are they assessed and what are the priorities? Is there an application cutoff time, and how is it determined? How much weight is given to such matters as the order in which the application was made, initiative shown, recommendations by various agencies, family income, number of dependants, ability to meet commitments, source of income, credit rating, current housing situation and any interrelationship between applicants? I feel that it is of the utmost importance to have objective and equitable guidelines for this crucial stage of the program, especially in smaller communities where adequate public knowledge and consultation is fundamental to the effective working of such a program.
The concept of any such program and the methods to be followed in its implementation must be comprehensive, objective, fair and make common sense if the program is to work. If one family is struggling hard to keep their home as their expenses increase faster than their income, a program whereby another family in the community is provided with a new subsidized home is bound to create controversy unless managed in a most convincing way. With today's economy and tight housing situation, many beleagured taxpayers trying to keep their homes find it hard to be convinced about such programs because of many of the concerns and problems I have just raised.
I have seen many of these concerns raised at meetings in Madoc and Marmora where people attend from other areas with similar questions concerning the rural and native housing program. Residents of the target area were quite concerned over various aspects of the program such as type of housing selection, availability and applicant selection. During one meeting, a friend and local politician suffered a heart attack and passed away after expressing his feelings on the program. Another politician resigned his post, and a local election of officers resulted to fill council vacancies.
I have been contacted by constituents expressing their concerns on the program as planned for various areas in the riding. Many of the concerns are over topics I have already mentioned, and go to stress the necessity of suitable guidelines and an appropriate program in tune with the economic times if Canadians are to be convinced of the program and if it is to operate effectively and efficiently.
Public consultation, input and acceptance is important to the functioning of such programs in small municipalities, and
February 8, 1982

it is usually more acceptable for the public to find out things first-hand rather than by rumours. People like to be made aware of the implications of such programs, especially when they are subsidized by taxpayers' money.
Canada is facing severe economic problems right now, and a housing shortage is one of the aspects of the poor state of the economy. The latest budget did little to help Canadians, many of whom continue to struggle in an uphill battle to get ahead. There is a need for federal programs and assistance to get the economy moving again. There is also the need for a comprehensive housing policy to aid various levels of Canadians struggling to acquire or maintain shelter. Such policies must realize the seriousness of the problems facing the country when hardworking families are having a hard time keeping their homes. Programs must be assessed and reassessed to take into account the problems, needs and concerns of all Canadians if they are to be effective and respected in practice. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Celine Hervieux-Payette (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate having this opportunity to speak before the House this evening, especially after publicly announcing my interest in the construction industry this weekend. In fact, I should like to point out that although my colleagues from central and eastern Montreal and I may have asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to add further measures to assist the construction industry, our request to the Prime Minister should not be interpreted as a criticism of the bill now before the House, which has my full support.
To me, this bill is extremely important for the operation and administration of the mortgage insurance fund. It will help the government and the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to be more effective in the area of public mortgage insurance. However, 1 should like to focus on the social aspects of the bill. Bill C-89 is important because it deals directly with two urgent social problems, namely, renewal of mortgage loans and rental accommodation. The bill is also a tool for dealing with other social problems. It enables the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to facilitate the provision of mortgage loans that are adapted to periods when mortgage rates fluctuate considerably. These loans offer greater security with respect to monthly payments, so that people can still consider purchasing a home as a way of increasing their security and providing for their retirement years.
The bill will help to ensure that the mortgage funds required in the long term will be available on the market. I agree with the minister that the bill does not reproduce all his plans for the housing sector. It is a start in the right direction, but again I agree with the minister that we must go further and deal with the problems of rural and native housing and low-income tenants. In fact, in a few weeks I shall be celebrating, with the
Housing
people of my constituency, to mark the acquisition of several hundred co-operative housing units by the citizens of the riding of Montreal-Mercier. We have here a federal government program that is helping low-income people to become home owners. Mr. Speaker, it would not be fair to hold up this bill too long because of the provisions it does not contain, since the minister has clearly indicated his intention of dealing with other problems in due time. Members will recall that the decision to set up the plan was first announced in the budget speech by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on November 12. In fact, the previous speaker was asking the minister to elaborate on the programs. Mr. Speaker, I feel that those who attend the proceedings of this House have several times witnessed the indignation and outrage shown by opposition members when the minister made his announcement, and this evening, the same members are asking us to announce the details of these programs. So, Mr. Speaker, what else can I do, except commend a bill aimed at helping our fellow citizens. The first aspect of the bill, Mr. Speaker, is a security provided by the government to those lenders willing to allow home owners with liquidity problems to delay payment of the interest on their mortgage loan. Would-be eligible home owners who must pay more than 30 per cent of the household's gross income in principal, interests and taxes and, as the case may be, half of joint condominium charges. Consequently, those people would have a substantial equity in their home, in that the home has a much higher value than the amount still outstanding on the mortgage loan. The above-mentioned plan will allow them to use their equity to solve their liquidity problems.
This arrangement is not available to everyone. Thus, individuals who do not have a substantial equity in their home, for example, the co-owners of a condominium unit whose value has decreased throughout the years could not resort to that solution. To those who only have a small equity in their home and who have to repay more than 30 per cent of their income in monthly payments, the plan provides a direct grant of up to $3,000.
Mr. Speaker, I am aware that many hon. members have received letters and phone calls from their constituents who are anxious to know whether the plan would apply to their particular circumstances and how they could take advantage of it. Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation officials who administer the scheme advise people to first contact their lenders. These lenders, I mean the banks, trust companies, credit unions, etc., which grant mortgage loans, are aware of the terms and conditions of the plan and have the application forms. They are ready to discuss this plan with their borrowers and help them decide whether they are eligible for the assistance provided by way of insurance or a grant, as well as fill out the application form. This form is then sent to a branch of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. CMHC officials advise me that they have already received a number of

February 8, 1982
Housing
applications, but they will not be in a position to offer either insurance or a grant as long as this bill which is now before the House has not been passed and as long as Parliament has not empowered it to act. As everybody knows, Mr. Speaker, there are measures provided for in the MacEachen budget, but for this program to be implemented, this bill must be passed by the House.
There are a few facts which people interested in this scheme should know. First of all, only those who own their own homes and live in them are eligible. For instance, a home owner could not obtain either insurance or a grant for a second house which he is renting out to others or which is occupied by members of his family. However, if he occupies an apartment a duplex or a triplex he owns, he will be deemed to be the home owner occupying that apartment for the purpose of this program. The assistance will apply to only one mortgage, either the first, second or any other, whichever the borrower chooses, on condition this mortgage loan was obtained when the house was bought. Of course, the assistance would apply to only one mortgage renewal. The grants will be paid to the lender on behalf of the borrower and not directly to the latter. It is understood that these grants would be tax free.
Mr. Speaker, I have made it clear to my constituents that a cheque will not be addressed directly to the home owner who is experiencing difficulties but that the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation will send one to the lending institution after it has approved the application.
To decide whether or not the income of a borrower makes him eligible for assistance under this bill, the income of the whole family before taxes is taken into account. That is, the income of the wife and husband, as well as other sources of income such as rental income, investment income, family allowances. As l have said before, the mortgage lenders are quite willing to discuss the program with their clients. I can even say that the willingness with which lending institutions have lent a hand with the application of the program has been of great value to the public. Because they have agreed to assume part of the administration of the plan by screening applications for assistance and putting up the funds, those institutions have enabled the government to make substantial savings in terms of costs and man-years.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I must emphasize that the Liberal government has always respected that long-standing tradition between the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the Canadian lending institutions, and co-operated with the private sector to bolster our economy and, of course, the housing sector as well.
Naturally the plan has come under criticism, particularly because it has failed to find a lasting solution to the problems of Canadians who occupy their own homes and who are faced with the difficult rearrangement of their personal expenditures as a result of soaring interest rates. Still we must admit that the program plan does meet its objective which is to help those
people who may lose their home owing to high interest rates. I should even add, Mr. Speaker, that the plan offers that assistance in such a way as to make it possible to take into consideration at the same time the restraint which the government must use in the administration of public funds in these trying times and, of course, the urge to help the home owner keep the house on which he has already made sizeable payments.
The Canada mortgage renewal plan is an adequate answer to the problem of the current economic situation. It is a major feature of the bill introduced in the House, and I urge my colleagues to study it very carefully and diligently. The Canada mortgage renewal plan amounts to a fair solution of the problems inherent in renewing mortgages. Generally speaking, owners living in their own home earn appreciably higher incomes than renters do and, something which is just as significant, they have much larger assets than renters do. An over-all assistance program for mortgage renewals would be extremely costly, of course, and it would have transferred the income of small-wage earners to others who are much better off. It would then have been very difficult to reconcile such a program with the will of the government to help the most needy.
This is why in 1979 1 so strongly opposed Bill C-20. The program was very unfair. It promoted subsidies and grants for everyone. This, of course, was to be done using the money for those who cannot afford a property.
[ Translation]
However, the government realized that the tendency of mortgage terms to get increasingly shorter has caused great uncertainty among home owners. Mortgage renewal can affect in many ways the wellbeing of families and create cash problems. Mortgage renewal has been a source of uncertainty both for existing and prospective home owners and rental housing contractors. Confidence is very low, Mr. Speaker, and measures will have to be taken to renew confidence. The Canada mortgage renewal plan helps reduce uncertainty in households that are or will be renewing their mortgages. Other steps no doubt will be needed later, and I am ready to discuss them at other times.
Numerous discussions have dealt directly with the current mortgage instrument problems, namely, their short term, which generally is one year, and their uncertainty. Many people have urged that this instrument be changed. Home owner associations suggested we should come back to a 25-year mortgage term, because it would give families the certainty of being able to meet their monthly payments. Home owners want the assurance they will be able to meet their payments. With that security, families can plan for years ahead. However, Mr. Speaker, I am not sure the current
February 8, 1982

global and North American economic situation can make such a program possible. And at any rate, I am not sure either that a return to a 25-year term would necessarily solve the problem, such a plan would transfer to investors the uncertainty pertaining to interest rate fluctuations, which finally would lead to a reduced supply of mortgage funds. Other solutions have been put forward, for instance, variable rate loans, loans with capital gain participation, loans with indexed principal. 1 am not sure these proposals will succeed, but they certainly deserve to be put to the test, and it will take time for the market to accept them. That is why I am happy that Bill C-89 enables the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to propose those types of mortage loans in order that present and future home owners may take advantage of them if they so decide.
Mr. Speaker, it is not possible to consider the social impact of this legislation or the broader question of housing without dealing with rental housing. This is an area I am quite aware of, because the constituency of Montreal-Mercier probably includes a majority of renters. All members of the House are concerned with the supply of rental housing and the problems faced by low-income renters in tight markets.
Earlier, I mentioned the co-op housing program and noted that this was a formula introduced by the Liberal government to allow low-wage earners to become home owners. Mr. Speaker, I believe that this program has proven effective and 1 am happy that the residents of the Mercier riding can benefit from it. Moreover, the Canadian government will finance 40,000 new rental units in 1982, including 25,000 units under the non-profit and co-op housing programs, which provide housing for low and middle-income tenants. In addition, the Canada rental supply plan will finance another 15,000 units to prevent a worsening of the shortage of rental housing. The bill will play a major role in providing these 15,000 units by enabling the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to insure more substantial loans for rental housing.
Mr. Speaker, we are facing four major social problems: the first is that of the availability and supply of rental housing at reasonable prices. In this regard, the bill now before the House will help to ensure that the 15,000 rental units announced in the budget will prevent a further deterioration of the markets which are faced with a rental housing shortage. No one will claim that this bill will solve every housing problem in Canada, but I believe that it is a positive beginning and this is why I support the minister's efforts and this bill. The commitment entered upon by the government is obvious if we consider the 25,000 non-profit or co-op housing units to be built in 1982.
The second problem concerns low-income tenants throughout the country. Through its non-profit and co-op housing programs, the government has shown its concern for these people. The minister has also expressed support for a housing allowance program and his wish to consider this proposal at length.
Hons inf;
The third problem, Mr. Speaker, is the lack of confidence or the uncertainty which besets present and future occupant home owners. The Canada mortgage renewal plan and the provisions of this bill, which will allow CMHC to help develop new forms of mortgage loans, are aimed at solving this problem. In any case, Mr. Speaker, 1 want to take this opportunity to remind hon. members that it would be a complete fraud to pretend to solve all of Canada's economic problems with the introduction of such a bill. This is why I invite my colleagues in the opposition to consider this positive measure, to try to improve its content, but also to approve it as soon as possible since our constituents are anxious to see it passed quickly.
The fourth problem, Mr. Speaker, concerns the miserable housing conditions of our native and rural population. As I came from a rural area before settling down in an urban area, Mr. Speaker, I must say that 1 am aware that the housing situation is indeed distressing and in this respect agree with my colleagues across the aisle. However, I do not believe that this is a good reason to prevent or delay the implementation of such a bill. If we are aware of problems in other sectors, Mr. Speaker, other action could be taken, and this is why 1 urge my colleagues to support this bill. 1 believe that the government has shown concern for the native people, the problems of employment and the rural situation. With respect to financing, we have had the previous bill on Canagrex, and I believe that this government has shown no reluctance in supporting positive action to help the Canadian people.
I think that a short discussion of this bill is needed. I hope that my colleagues will support Bill C-89. Although 1 recognize it is the role of the opposition to oppose, they should also take part in discussions and approval of measures.
This is a very positive measure. I believe that Canadians can afford this program and approve these measures, and it is my hope that we will vote on this important bill shortly.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT OF CANADA-TRANSFER OF TOURISM OFFICE FROM OTTAWA TO YARMOUTH, N.S. (B) ADVICE TENDERED BY MINISTER
GOVERNMENT OF CANADA-TRANSFER OF TOURISM OFFICE FROM OTTAWA TO YARMOUTH, N.S. (B) ADVICE TENDERED BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, until November 30, 1981, the main ingredients of the government's decentralization policy were patronage, lack of respect for the taxpayers' dollar, political advantage to a particular ministry and secrecy.
On that day, as a result of two questions to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) and the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) on the proposed move of the distribution unit of the Canadian Government Tourism Office, two new elements were added-stupidity and weakness.
Lest you think, Mr. Speaker, that I am too hard on these two hon. gentlemen, I should tell the House the facts. Let me begin by saying that it is now common knowledge that in stopping the decentralization program in 1979, the Clark government saved the Canadian taxpayer approximately $250 million and eliminated countless negative effects on the delivery of government services to the people of Canada. I presume that if this government had asked for the same advice on costs and efficiency from the same public service, it would have received the same advice as our government received. Therefore, the present policy must be based on political advantage, and lack of respect for the taxpayers' dollars, laced with a generous amount of patronage. But there is more, and this is where stupidity and weakness enter.
In 1977, before the Clark government stopped the move, the Minister of State for Small Businesses advised the President of the Treasury Board not to move the tourism distribution unit to Yarmouth. Again, on April 29, 1981, in a letter that the Minister of State for Small Businesses admitted writing to the President of the Treasury Board-which everyone can see if they ask-the minister pleaded an eloquent case against the move. He recalled the consistent advice against the move over the years, related how the standard of service would be lowered and described the distribution centre as much more than a warehousing operation; rather, a sophisticated office with national and international responsibilities to get Canada's message out within a critical delivery component. He detailed how the move to Yarmouth would increase the costs of the operation, impose time penalties on the service and agreed that if there was a strong case against the move to Yarmouth in 1977, there was an even stronger case in 1981, and certainly stronger today.
Only in Ottawa, only within the Treasury Board could such foolishness abound. For example, a distribution unit is to be moved where no postal workers will be available. Material which should be out in the marketplace will have to be stored in the post office in Halifax. These delays will mean missing media deadlines. Agents, embassies and offices abroad will suffer from unco-ordinated shipments, and cost increases will be enormous. For example, with regard to provincial costs, Ontario provided 124,000 pounds of literature in the past twelve months at a shipping cost of $3,200. The Yarmouth cost would be $17,240. British Columbia provided 53,000 pounds at a cost of $9,600. That cost would climb to $15,565. Some might grow fainthearted in the face of this logic and the good sense of the letter, but no one should ever accuse the government of faintheartedness when it comes to stupidity. It embraces stupidity in a manner which is truly breathtaking. The Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism recognized stupidity for what it was and admitted it to the House. He said he wrote the letter; he did not agree with the move; it would make him a laughing stock; and he asked for another unit to be moved. When I read that, I said there was a glimmer of hope for this poor benighted creature. However, seconds later, he dashed this slim glimmer of hope to the ground. He said, and this is where he demonstrated his weakness: "Please save me from the member from Yarmouth. She is thrashing me to death with her purse. Find me another unit for Yarmouth. I can't stand it." Another unit could not be found, so he changed his mind, and what was ridiculous, what was irrelevant, and what was stupid before now became the order of the day for government business.
Even this tired, listless, weak-willed, patronage-ridden and ramshackle excuse for a government has to account to the people at some time. Let it do so now. Let it produce all the correspondence. The parliamentary secretary is here. Let him produce all the correspondence and the studies on decentralization. Let the government find that other department or unit to go to Yarmouth. Nobody disagrees with the federal presence in Yarmouth, but how can the government fly in the face of a move which has been condemned by everyone and even by the minister himself? Who is in charge over there? What establishes the rule over there? Is it good sense; is it patronage; is it the appropriate delivery of government service; or is it the hon. member for South West Nova (Miss Campbell) or the public interest? Find another unit, please, Mr. Speaker, even if you have to intervene personally. It is painful for me to have to sit here day after day and to see the government make such a fool of itself.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: GOVERNMENT OF CANADA-TRANSFER OF TOURISM OFFICE FROM OTTAWA TO YARMOUTH, N.S. (B) ADVICE TENDERED BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat shocked to hear some of the adjectives used by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) because when we look at the employment rate of that area of Nova Scotia and compare it with that here in the nation's capital, we note that it is over 4 per cent higher than here in central Canada. There are, therefore, humanitarian reasons behind this move, and humanitarian reasons behind moves to other areas in the
February 8, 1982

Atlantic region which do not enjoy the opportunities we enjoy here in central Canada. Part of the decision was based on the need for decentralization so we could be in closer contact with people in outlying areas. We should look at this matter in the true Canadian context of sharing. We must provide the people of that area with a standard of living comparable to that in the nation's capital. I hope this is one move in that direction. We should not be greedy and hold everything in central Canada. We should be willing to share.
Work is proceeding on the Canadian Government Office of Tourism facility in Yarmouth, Nova Scotia. Completion of the new structure and occupancy is scheduled for 1983. Officials of the office of tourism have had several meetings with officials of the city, Canada Post and the Department of Employment and Immigration, to ensure the transition is done as smoothly as possible so as not to inconvenience people seeking travel information and literature on Canada. Transportation companies, including CP Transport, have been asked for plans and estimates of costs for moving the tourist information to the Yarmouth distribution centre. Officials of the Canadian Government Office of Tourism also met with Canada Post officials in Halifax recently and were assured of the fullest co-operation possible. A postal plan for servicing Yarmouth will be presented to the CGOT shortly to allow time for the new Crown corporation to settle in.
Meetings have also been held in Yarmouth with Employment and Immigration Canada in relation to possible staffing requirements for the new facility. Here in Ottawa a professional career counsellor is advising those employees of the distribution centre who will be relocating in the national capital area on retraining, job rotation and relocation.
The Canadian government wants to decentralize, and, in view of the high unemployment figures in the Yarmouth area compared with those in the city of Ottawa, I do not think we should be complaining but, rather, trying to help those people who are disadvantaged.

subtopic: THE ECONOMY-QUERY RESPECTING MATTERS CONSIDERED WHEN PREPARING BUDGET. (B) DURATION OF RECESSION
THE ECONOMY-QUERY RESPECTING MATTERS CONSIDERED WHEN PREPARING BUDGET. (B) DURATION OF RECESSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks tonight centre on a question I put to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on December 9 of last year. At that time I was pointing out to him that, in the absence of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, (Mr. Gray) in the House, 1 felt he should inform the House concerning the plight of some 140,000 people who the Canadian Manufacturers' Association had indicated only that day had lost their jobs over the last three months. The emperor was in one of his snarky moods that day and simply said "I will be very happy to convey the hon. member's representations to the minister; I believe he will be in the House presently." I followed up my question by asking would he indicate why he and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce had put us in the place where we were experiencing such a serious recession in Canada. The emperor
Adjournment Debate
then came back and said that he could not agree with that premise and that he had no answer to give.
The reason I have reiterated the question and the two answers is that I think that in reality this government does not fully realize the hardship it is creating in this country. The CMA people at that time indicated that 140,000 people had lost their jobs. As we know, within the last week the president of the CMA is now saying that it may be 400,000 Canadians who will be out of work as a result of the present recession we are in.
The Prime Minister may feel he can quibble with our words. He may feel he can say that it is technically not a recession, but every economist in Canada would disagree with him. The fact is that for the last four years this country has had a negative real growth on a per capita basis in each of those four years.
Let me not ask you to accept my figures, Mr. Speaker. In the October issue of the internationally well regarded magazine Euromoney, it was pointed out that Canada among world countries had an economic performance between 1974 and 1981 ranking number thirtieth. That means we ranked after countries such as Taiwan, Singapore, Hong Kong, Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, Iraq, Egypt, Thailand, Cyprus, Japan, Korea, Burma, Paraguay, India, Honduras, Libya, Pakistan, Indonesia, Tunisia, Trinidad and Tobago, The Philippines, Panama, Guatemala, Ecuador, United States of America, Norway, Germany, Austria, Malawi-and then Canada.
I mention this because I think it is time that not only the emperor himself but his ministers, those dwarf ministers that surround him, somehow accepted the plight they have caused in the country. We have a competitively high inflation level in Canada. In fact, the same economic review I have referred to, the October issue of Euromoney, says that as far as inflation is concerned we have the nineteenth worst inflation level they record. As far as economic growth in those years is concerned, 1974 to 1981, we ranked forty-eighth.
I am suggesting to the House this evening that, bearing in mind the riches we have in this country, the resources that we have, the agricultural produce and capability we have, our talented people, and the proximity we have to the wealthiest market in the world, it is time the government accepted the challenge to make us number one again among world nations.
This is why I am suggesting, since we have now slipped into a recession, that the Prime Minister should offer some explanation not only to the House but to the people of Canada. He should be willing to tell us why, in terms of personal wealth, for example, we have slipped behind Switzerland which now has personal wealth for every man, woman and child of $14,240 in United States dollars. He should be willing to tell us why we are behind Luxembourg with $12,820 in personal earnings; Sweden with $11,920; Denmark, $11,900; Germany, $11,730; Belgium, $10,890; United States, $10,820; Norway, $10,710; Iceland, $10,490; The Netherlands, $10,240; France,

February 8, 1982
Adjournment Debate
$9,940. Then comes Canada! We used to be a proud No. 2 on the list. How come the emperor has allowed us to sink so low?

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Frith (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Deputy Leader of the Government in the Senate
subtopic: THE ECONOMY-QUERY RESPECTING MATTERS CONSIDERED WHEN PREPARING BUDGET. (B) DURATION OF RECESSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, several points were raised by the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) with which I will deal in the order he presented them. Originally the hon. member asked his question on December 9, 1981. In his preamble he said to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau):
In view of the fact that we are now faced with the worst red ink figures in our relationship with the rest of the world in terms of trade-
Then he went on to ask why we were in the same situation in terms of losing jobs; basically that was the question he asked.
If one listened to the rhetoric of the question, one would assume that in fact our trade balance in 1981 was the worst on record. In fact, the way it was worded one would think there was a trade deficit in 1981. Yet the figures show that in 1981, despite the fact that the hon. member quoted from Euromoney, the economic review, Canada had a $6.5 billion trade surplus. Admittedly that is not quite as good as the record of 1980. I remind the hon. member that there was still a Liberal government on this side of the House when Canada had its largest trade surplus in history of $7.8 billion. If one listened only to the rhetoric of the hon. member opposite, one would think that the country was faced with a trade deficit, and the facts prove the opposite.
In 1981, in terms of trade, had the fourth quarter or the last quarter of that year been projected on a yearly basis, the result would have shown an even better record trade surplus between Canada and its major trading partners in the world. Evidently the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Lumley) has done an excellent job in terms of promoting Canadian products. This shows up in our trade surplus with other markets.
In addition, the hon. member asked why Canada was doing so poorly when we were in such close proximity to the wealthiest market in the world. I would assume by that he meant the United States. It is fair to say that roughly 70 per cent of all exported Canadian products are traded with the United States. The hon. member opposite would be in agreement with me that the United States is in its worst recessionary period since the post war period as well. It should be borne in mind that when 70 per cent of everything produced in the country goes to the United States, whose economy is in trouble as well, that the Canadian economy will be in trouble. With the budget and by some of the measures we have introduced we are trying to alleviate the unemployment situation to which the hon. member referred. I am confident that as the United States economy turns around, we will find the economy of Canada will correspond in a like manner.

subtopic: HEALTH-REQUEST FOR VACCINATION PROGRAM TO COMBAT RED MEASLES
HEALTH-REQUEST FOR VACCINATION PROGRAM TO COMBAT RED MEASLES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on November 20, 1981, my question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare was phrased as follows:
A disease which is seriously underrated by the public and also by some health workers, as far as morbidity is concerned, and one that can and does cause significant brain damage, is red measles. This serious virus infection is preventable by vaccination. The United States is committed to a national vaccination program, with a goal of completely eliminating the disease arising within that country by 1982. Does the Minister of National Health and Welfare have any plans to stimulate and co-ordinate such a program in Canada where the responsibility for health rests with the provinces?
The Minister of National Health and Welfare answered:
Madam Speaker, the jurisdiction for implementing such health policy remains with the provincial health authorities. However, the fact is that the National Advisory Committee on Immunization which prepared guidelines for the eradication of measles in Canada strongly recommended that legislation be enacted in each of the ten provinces requiring measle immunization prior to school entry. Unfortunately it has not been implemented in some parts of Canada. I do not have the direct power to do it, so I guess an occasion such as this to tell the public is of value.
My purpose in bringing this question to the attention of the minister again is because I fee! this is an important issue and one which focuses on the physical wellbeing of all Canadians and our progeny.
The urgency of this situation is heightened by the fact that in 1980 the reported rate of measles in Canada was approximately ten times higher than in the United States. In Canada there were 13,750 cases, having a rate of 58 per 100,000 population; whereas in the U.S.A. there were 13,430 cases (the rate being 6 per 100,000 population).
It was estimated that approximately 2,500 Canadians were infected with red measles in 1981. While this figure is down considerably from previous years, it becomes less impressive when we realize that only 2,347 measle cases were reported in the entire United States during the first 26 weeks of 1981. What we must all realize is that we have reached a point where we can eliminate this infectious disease. Red measles has hitherto been referred to in Canada as a common childhood disease. It is not by any yardstick a benign disease. Complications such as middle-ear infection and bronchopneumonia occur in one out of every 15 cases. Inflammation of the brain or encephalitis occurs in one out of every 1,000 cases of measles. This condition leaves some with permanent brain damage and others with residual paralysis. Mental retardation occurs once in every 3,000 cases sometimes due to a result of the encephalitis. The disease can be eradicated but in order to do so a 100 per cent comprehensive program of public, not private, vaccination is required.
In June, 1981, the Canadian Paediatric Society passed a resolution promoting a more universal use of the vaccine to immunize citizens against the disease. The National Advisory Committee for Immunization has continually made similar recommendations. In addition, the Canadian Medical Association in August, 1981, recommended compulsory vaccinations to eradicate this disease. Implementation of such a program is
February 8, 1982

the responsibility of the provincial legislature. The response to these submissions has not been favourable in any province except the province of New Brunswick.
Compare this response with that in the United States where all 50 states have such legislation in force. There, children must have a certificate in order to be admitted to school and if a case of measles breaks out, all members of the school must show an immunization record as proof of having been vaccinated. If no such proof is available, they are excluded from school. It is only through well supervised programs of this nature that the 1982 goal of completely eliminating the disease within that country will be realized.
Relating this back to Canada, Mr. Speaker, since supplies of the vaccine are already available at the provincial level it seems to me that the federal government's role should not only entail providing educational information and encouraging universal acceptance of vaccination programs, especially those relating to certain age groups, but it should also be encouraging the remainder of the provinces to enact legislation which would facilitate the degree of control now being achieved over the disease in the United States. In this way we would be encouraging a national health strategy to eliminate indigenous measles in Canada. A commitment must be made by the federal government to do this.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Frith (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Deputy Leader of the Government in the Senate
subtopic: HEALTH-REQUEST FOR VACCINATION PROGRAM TO COMBAT RED MEASLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I just begin by saying that the minister is in agreement with everything the hon. member has said in his preamble. I think the hon. member has correctly pointed out the saddest situation that can arise, which is when the government or the medical profession has the wherewithal and the weapons to eliminate disease and we Find these are not being used properly. From a
Adjournment Debate
medical practitioner's standpoint, that is one of the saddest things in terms of trying to educate the public.
As an example of that, Mr. Speaker, the major commitment of the World Health Organization in the 1970s was to eradicate smallpox on a worldwide scale. From the medical practitioner's standpoint, one realizes that that is much more difficult in terms of immunization than it would be in the case of measles. I think basically what we have to do as a national government is educate the Canadian public as to the ease with which we can eliminate or eradicate the incidence of measles in Canada. We have to begin by educating the parents to have their youngsters undergo vaccination prior to their entering school, or at least in their very early school years.
The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Hudecki) points out quite correctly that roughly one in every 15 reported cases results in ear infections and pulmonary pneumonia. As he mentioned, we have severe brain inflammation in one out of every thousand cases. Even more important, we have records of several unnecessary deaths occurring in Canada in the last few years because young children contacted measles.
The minister has pointed out that the United States, on the other hand, in 1978 instituted a program to eliminate measles by the year 1982, and it has been rather successful. I just want to point out, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) will be meeting with her provincial counterparts in the next six to seven weeks and we hope to be able to convince those provincial ministers to institute compulsory immunization programs. That is the only way we are going to eradicate measles in this country.
